blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: An insurer's PolicyService has quote() and renew(), and each checks that the holder is at least 18 with the line `today.getYear() - birthYear >= 18`, written out in both methods. A ticket reports that people born late in the year were quoted while still 17, and the fix changes quote() to compare full birth dates with Period.between; a test for quote() is added and passes. A holder born on 2008-11-20 asks to renew on 2026-03-02. What does renew() do?

options.text: It refuses the renewal, since Period.between(2008-11-20, 2026-03-02) gives 17 years, and both methods now compute that
options.says: the fix changed quote() only; renew() holds its own copy of the rule, which still compares years

options.text: It refuses the renewal, since 2026-03-02 falls before the holder's 18th birthday on 2026-11-20
options.says: the date is before the birthday, but renew()'s copy of the rule compares years, not dates

options.text: It accepts the renewal, since its check subtracts 2008 from 2026, which gives 18
options.says: the rule was kept in two places and the fix reached the one the ticket named

options.text: It accepts the renewal, since 2026 - 2008 gives 18 in quote() as well, and both methods compute that
options.says: quote() now compares full dates and gives 17; only renew() still subtracts years

origin.section: A Rule Kept in Two Places Gets Fixed in One of Them

questions.stem: A shop treats coupon codes without regard to case. Its `apply(code)` returns `coupons.keySet().stream().anyMatch(c -> c.equalsIgnoreCase(code))` and changes nothing, and its `discountFor(code)` returns `coupons.get(code)`, where coupons is a HashMap<String, Integer> holding "WINTER10" -> 10. A shopper types "winter10", and apply() accepts it. What does discountFor("winter10") return?

options.text: It returns 10, since apply() has just accepted "winter10", and both methods read the same coupons map
options.says: reading the same map does not mean deciding equality the same way; get() compares keys with String.equals

options.text: It returns 10, since a String's hashCode is computed without regard to case, so get() reaches the "WINTER10" entry
options.says: String.hashCode depends on the case of each character

options.text: It returns null, since a String's hashCode and equals both depend on case, so get() finds no "winter10" entry
options.says: the map lookup is a copy of the rule that does not look like one, and it says the opposite of apply()

options.text: It returns null, since apply() removes a coupon from the map as soon as a shopper's code has matched it
options.says: apply() changes nothing in the map; get() misses the entry because it compares keys with String.equals

origin.section: A Copy of a Rule Doesn't Have to Look Like One

questions.stem: A library app, not yet launched and with no members stored, will store members in a HashMap under their card number as typed at sign-up, with or without spaces ("4410 2290" or "44102290"). borrow() and renew() find a member by looping over the keys and comparing `strip(k).equals(strip(card))`, where strip() removes spaces. More lookups by card are planned, and the team wants a design where a lookup written next year cannot disagree with these two without some test noticing. Which design is that?

options.text: Keys are the card as typed at sign-up, and every lookup is get(card) as typed, since the map then holds what members actually typed
options.says: get(card) on keys stored as typed treats "4410 2290" and "44102290" as different cards, so the rule about spaces is lost

options.text: Keys are the card as typed at sign-up, and every lookup is get(strip(card)), since strip() is where the rule about spaces is written
options.says: keys stored as typed still contain spaces, so a lookup that strips only its own input misses them

options.text: Keys are strip(card) at sign-up, and every lookup is get(strip(card)), since a card with spaces then never reaches the map
options.says: the rule sits in the key every path has to pass through, so a lookup that skips it misses the first card typed with spaces

options.text: Keys are strip(card) at sign-up, and every lookup is get(card) as typed, since the keys in the map then already have no spaces
options.says: a card typed with spaces at lookup is not stripped, so get() misses the stored key

origin.section: One Method Decides When Two Names Are the Same, and Every Path Calls It

questions.stem: A subscription service has `invoiceDue(issued)` returning `issued.plusDays(30)`, for payment terms, which finance sets, and `trialEnd(started)` returning `started.plusDays(30)`, for free trials, whose length marketing sets. In review, a colleague asks you to extract one `thirtyDaysAfter(date)` method that both call. What do you answer?

options.text: Extract it, since when finance moves payment terms to 45 days, one edit in thirtyDaysAfter() keeps free trials in step
options.says: that one edit would also change the trial length, which nobody asked for

options.text: Extract it, since when a third 30-day period joins payment terms and free trials, it can call thirtyDaysAfter() too
options.says: a third period is only the same rule if it must change whenever the others do; equal text is not enough

options.text: Keep both, since when finance moves payment terms to 45 days, free trials still run for 30 days
options.says: if one can change without the other, the equal lines are two rules that agree today

options.text: Keep both, since with only payment terms and free trials sharing the body, DRY asks for no change before a third copy
options.says: the number of copies does not decide it; the question is whether one must change when the other does

origin.section: Identical Lines Are One Rule Only If One Must Change When the Other Does

concepts: A copy of a rule need not look like one: a map lookup by the raw value decides equality with String.equals, and neither a text search nor a duplicate-code detector finds it.
A business rule kept in two places agrees with itself until the first fix or change, which reaches only the copy the report named, and the other copy keeps the defect.
Whether to merge two equal pieces of code is decided by asking whether one must change when the other does, not by whether their text is equal.
